az_main_wall_6.blurb:
The tallest and best-known wall in Jacks Canyon, a limestone gorge outside Winslow. The rock is pocketed and edgy, and nearly everything here is bolted. The grades cluster in the 5.11s and 5.12s, with a smaller group of 5.10s and a handful at 5.13 and up, so it suits a climber ready to push into the harder numbers. Sacrificial Lizard, Tales From the Grypt and Kindest Cut are among the standouts.

A clip stick is handy for some starts. Spring and fall are the comfortable seasons; summer pushes you into the shade, and winter can be cold though sunny afternoons warm the stone. The canyon floods in places after storms, and wet dirt on the access road turns to sticky mud.
az_main_wall_6.parking_note: Take the signed turn off Highway 87 south of Winslow, open and close the gate behind you, and follow the dirt road to its end near the pit toilet on the rim. Most cars make it when dry; after rain the road turns to deep mud.
az_main_wall_6.approach: A short trail leads from the rim parking down into the canyon to the wall.

az_west_side_2.blurb:
The west side of Winslow Wall, a secluded sandstone canyon cut by East Clear Creek south of Winslow. The rock is mostly solid and often carries a dark, hard patina. Trad lines tend to be steep splitter cracks, while the bolted routes involve patina crimps and technical face moves. Most climbs are single pitch and sit in the 5.11 to 5.13 range, with a smaller number of easier trad routes such as Kingsnake and Darkstar, and about two-thirds of the routes are sport.

There is no shade or shelter at the rim, so plan around heat and wind. You rappel in on fixed lines and climb out the gully or jug the ropes, so bring ascenders or a grigri and a 70 m rope.
az_west_side_2.parking_note: Drive east on Highway 99 from Highway 87 near Winslow, turn onto Territorial Road, then follow the dirt road past the fence, bearing left at the fork, to its end. Parts of the road cross private land, so go carefully and quietly.
az_west_side_2.approach: Follow the canyon rim about a third of a mile to a small slot, scramble down it to the fixed rappel and haul lines, and descend to the creek.

az_hobo_jungle.blurb:
A small, quiet crag on the northeast flank of the San Francisco Peaks, reached by dirt forest roads from Flagstaff. The rock is a good-quality volcanic stone, and the routes are mostly bolted face and steep wall climbing, with a few trad lines. It is often called a mini version of the main Peaks crag, and the grades are stacked in the 5.11s, with a decent handful of 5.10s and 5.12s and a couple of 5.13 test pieces such as Steel Reserve. Moderate climbers will find only a few easier lines.

The access roads are washboarded, and the wash below can flash flood.
az_hobo_jungle.parking_note: From Flagstaff take Highway 89 north, turn onto the forest roads toward the northeast side of the Peaks, and park at the hairpin pullout, which is also a popular campsite. The roads are rough and heavily washboarded.
az_hobo_jungle.approach: Head south on the old jeep track for about 15 minutes; the crag starts just across a wash, at its right-hand end.

az_1_the_left_wall.blurb:
The Left Wall is the east-facing end of the Waterfall, a columnar basalt amphitheater in Oak Creek Canyon. Almost all of it is crack and face trad, with splitters, blocky starts and committing moves. Grades run from 5.10 through 5.12, with just a couple of harder lines, so it is not a place for beginner leaders. Vertebrae, Spite and Malice and Giardia Crack are favorites.

The wall catches morning light and goes shady by afternoon, and the base can be overgrown. It sheds more loose rock than the rest of the cliff, especially after freeze-thaw and rain, so wear a helmet. A 70 m rope and a generous rack with multiple small cams are useful. Expect a creek crossing that can be hard in high water.
az_1_the_left_wall.parking_note: Park at the Encinoso day-use area on Highway 89A in Oak Creek Canyon, then step over the guardrail toward the creek.
az_1_the_left_wall.approach: Drop to the creek, boulder-hop across, and follow paths upstream along the east side through brush, boulders and roots to the wall. High water can make the crossing difficult.

ar_candy_mountain.blurb:
Candy Mountain is a sandstone sport area tucked into a wooded valley a short distance from Sam's Throne, in the Ozarks near Mt. Judea. Where Sam's Throne is mostly trad, this is a place for bolted lines, many of them tall. Most of the climbs fall between 5.10 and 5.12, with fewer easier ones, plus a small set of boulder problems. Willy Wonka, Gracious Grant and Wizard and Glass are among the favorites, and Styx and Powder Puff are good tests of 5.12.

Access is through the woods and down a ladder section, so allow time before the first climb. It is a good place to warm up on 5.10s and 5.11s before trying the harder walls.

ar_desoto_bouldering_area.blurb:
A bouldering area in the Mulberry Valley of northwest Arkansas, with boulders sitting right beside the road so there is essentially no approach. The problems are technical and reward body tension and careful footwork more than raw power. The grades are broad: most sit between VB and V3, a solid middle band is V4 to V6, and there are some harder problems up to V9, so most climbers can find a circuit. The Pizza Problem and Picasso are two of the better-known lines.

It is quiet compared with the busier Ozark spots. Bring pads and plan to share the roadside pullouts carefully.
ar_desoto_bouldering_area.parking_note: From the Highway 23 and Highway 215 junction, drive east on 215 for about 9.6 miles, turn left onto an unmarked dirt road, and go nearly two miles to the roadside pullouts.

ar_font_red.blurb:
The main bouldering zone at Cowell in the Arkansas Ozarks, a remote area of clean sandstone. It has a high concentration of quality problems, from V0 into the V8 to V10 range, with plenty in the middle grades. Le Beak, Rings of Uranus, Planet Earth and Center Spooge are the best known, and the area is often compared to Fontainebleau.

Fred's Cave, the Power Wall and the Invasion are short walks away, so it works as a base for a multi-day trip. There is camping beside the boulders but no toilets or other facilities, and hunters use the same area in season. Stock up in town, pack out your trash and keep your speed down on the dusty road.
ar_font_red.parking_note: From Highway 7 in Cowell, turn onto road 6560 (marked by a white house with tire and barrel signs) and follow it in; the boulder areas are reached from this road. Avoid private property and drive slowly.

ar_main_bluffline.blurb:
The main wall at Shepherd Springs, a shaded sandstone bluff near Lake Fort Smith in northwest Arkansas. Most routes are bolted, with a dozen or so trad lines and one aid line. The grades concentrate in the 5.11s and 5.12s, with a good spread of 5.9 and 5.10 and a few 5.13s. Shepherd's Arete, Bottom Feeder, Biscuits and Jam and the Stump Route are worth knowing.

Big trees keep the wall in shade, which helps in warm weather, though the air gets muggy in summer. Very few climbers show up, and some routes can be dirty or overgrown, so a brush is handy. The trailhead is a small pullout and a cairn, which is easy to miss.
ar_main_bluffline.parking_note: Take Shepherd Springs Road past the Lake Fort Smith State Park entrance; the pavement ends and the dirt road continues a short way to a small pullout on the right, across from a cairn on the left.
ar_main_bluffline.approach: A short uphill trail starts from the cairn on the north side of the road and ends at the base of Shepherd's Arete.
